To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the designation process of the Cairngorn National Park was a complex process, which was influenced by many factors, and which did not necessarily lead to a more democratic approach to decision-making.

The case of Scottish Devolution is an interesting one in that, although proponents argued that it would bring about a ‘New Politics’, the practices of governing that were developed in the process of creating the Cairngorm National Park were largely those of managerialism and not of democratisation.
the process of designation was dominated by the central state, and that the new institutions of devolved government had little impact on the process of designation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the practice of governing has been reconfigured through devolution and how this has affected the politics of governing.
the ways in which the practices of governing are shaped by political rationalities.
the relationship between the politics of constitutional change and the practice of government.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new politics of devolution is not a new politics of participation, but a new politics of management.
the case study of the Cairngorn National Park demonstrates that, while there is some evidence of democratisation, the dominant rationality of governing remains that of managerialism.
, although the case of the Cairngorns national park does not provide an example of enhanced democratisation, it does not provide a counterexample either.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
devolution is a political rationality which has a democratic form but which, in practice, has a managerialist content.
the new politics is more of a continuation than a rupture.
devolution has not brought about a new politics of governing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the practice of governing in a devolved Scotland is not markedly different from that of governing under the previous centralising regime.

the practices of governing are shaped by a number of factors, not least of which are the political rationalities of the governing institutions, and the political context within which governing takes place.
the practices of devolution are not necessarily more democratic than previous practices of government.
